en: // The Chapter on Mindfulness //
The First Daily Lesson.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 1, Section 49. Now, memory (*smṛti*) is defined: "Memory is a cognition produced solely from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*);
this is its definition.
[Objection: But surely memory is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that [this is not so] because its object does not exist, because it is not a direct experience, and because error is possible, we say: no.
Because the validity of mere memory was refuted in the first chapter,
because external objects are observed to be uncontradicted,
and because it would entail the contradiction of inferences and other cognitions whose objects are past or future.
Because it would contradict all worldly experience; because it would entail the consequence of memory occurring even for an object never previously experienced;
and because, even if memory itself were self-luminous, it remains dependent on latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and other factors regarding the form of the object to be known.

If it is argued that [recognition] lacks validity because it apprehends its object only by bringing forward a previous experience, we say no; for such [prior experience] is absent in the case of memory-lapse (*smṛtipramoṣa*),
yet it is present in recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which is universally accepted as a valid means of knowledge.
If it is argued that [conceptual cognition] lacks validity because it is dependent on something else, we say no; for dependence upon its own causes is universal to all cognitions,
and being rooted in experience or being rooted in a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is inconclusive with respect to conceptual cognitions and the like.
Because being produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) is not a unique [defining characteristic],
and because even memory possesses independence regarding the manifestation and linguistic usage of its own object;
and if it is argued that there is dependence regarding the restriction of the object— just as in the case of desire and so forth— that is not so.
For otherwise, it would follow that [the Lord] is ignorant;
indeed, you maintain that knowledge itself is inherently directed toward its object.
For this very reason, you assert that even the eternal will and effort of the Lord require knowledge in order to determine their objects.
We also accept that desire and the other mental states possess, by their very nature, an inclination toward objects and the quality of being cognition.
If it is objected, "But this is like the case of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)," we say no;
for even that [impression] has a nature capable of producing a cognition that possesses an object identical to its own cause.
Therefore, it is established that [memory] has as its object only what is determined by its cause;
and this is the same even in the case of direct experience (*anubhava*).

Thus, for the dull-witted, the conventional distinction between dependence and independence regarding memory and direct experience is based merely on whether or not they are produced from an experience having the same object.
Even in the determination of one's own validity and so forth, there is no insistence on dependence upon experience;
for that [validity] is established through the illumination of its own object, the absence of sublation, and so on,
since the property of apprehending only what has already been apprehended is not unique [to perception].

Furthermore, there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of inference and so forth for the Prābhākaras; in the case of continuous cognitions (dhārāvāhika-jñāna) and so forth for the Naiyāyikas and others; in the case of the second moment of yogic perception and so forth for those who maintain the existence of an omniscient being perfected through yoga; and in the case of the non-eternal knowledge of God for certain proponents of God.
If it is argued that [perception] lacks authority because it is purposeless, we say no.
Because [the reason] is inconclusive due to grass and other objects being perceived by ants and the like,
and because it is unestablished;
for indeed, the accomplishment of the world's inspection of what has been done and what remains to be done is achieved through memory alone.
For it is through memory alone that verbal testimony and inference function,
as well as the accomplishment of devotion to others and so forth.
If it is argued that these purposes belong only to what was previously experienced, [we reply:]...
Why could they not be the very volition of Brahman, which is the primordial cause of the entire world?
And thus, even experience does not establish that [external object], because it can be said that experience has that [volition] as its cause.

As it is said in the *Prajñāparitrāṇa*: "Because its nature consists in the knowledge of what has already been known, and because it has abandoned its own object of cognition, memory is considered to lack validity even though it does not deviate from its object."
Such [objections] as these have also been refuted by this [argument].
If it is argued that [a cognition] lacks validity because there is an absence of the practical application of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no;
for the absence of the practical application of ordinary people (*pāmara*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The same applies to the existence of the activity of all investigators,
because it is itself subject to dispute, and because the non-existence of the activity of all investigators is unproven.
This is because the authority of works such as the *Mānamanohara* has been asserted by Vāgīśvara and others;
because the mere absence of usage by a few investigators leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
and because we do not hold the usages or non-usages of Akṣapāda and others in particularly high regard, just as we do not regard the usages of Bṛhaspati and others.
However, because there is universal consensus and no contradiction regarding [the authorship] of Indra-pāṇini and others, they are respected; whereas,
since Pārāśarya and others do not fall within the scope of the enumeration of authoritative sources (*pramāṇa*), their non-mention is irrelevant,
as there is no common usage even of the phrase "scripture (*āgama*) is an authoritative source."

Furthermore, in passages such as "Perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions," it is logical that there is no separate treatment for a Smṛti rooted in perception and so forth, because it shares the same status as perception and the other means of knowledge.
Thus, a Smṛti caused by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is itself indeed a means of valid cognition.
"Because of non-contradiction.

And it has been stated in the *Nyāyatattva*, in the fourth section (*adhikaraṇa*) which distinguishes between memory and indeterminate cognition: "Neither of the two [memory and indeterminate cognition] lacks a basis in a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
for since there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the qualification 'a means of valid knowledge is that which apprehends an object not yet apprehended' is inappropriate [to apply to them]."
"Where has the impossibility of a further cognition (*pramiti*) in respect of what is already cognized (*pramita*) been observed?
If you say 'in memory' (*smṛti*), then the thesis itself would be the example;
if you say 'in another cognition,' I do not grant that," and so forth.
And in the *Tattvaratnākara*: "The wise hold that valid cognition (*māna*) is a determination in accordance with reality (*yathārtha-niścaya*) and its cause;
there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to memory (*smṛti*), for memory is not a valid cognition because it lacks [determination] in accordance with reality."
Having said this, it is also stated in the commentary on its latter half: "Memory is the non-losing of an experienced object;
for example, 'that jar exists.
[Objection: But does the definition not also extend to that [memory]?"
True;
there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) in its pervasion, because that too is included within the class of things to be defined (lakṣyapakṣa).
“How can a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) be applied to that which is both definable and indefinable, or to that which is beyond definition?
For the wise know that worldly cognition and conventional usage have as their limits the definable and the indefinable.”
And so forth.

As for that which was stated by Śrī Viṣṇucitta as if to suggest that recollection lacks validity—namely, "Experience is a means of valid cognition; experience is knowledge distinct from recollection," and so on—
That is certainly by way of conforming to the highest [Mīmāṃsaka] position.
For this very reason, they have acted otherwise at the stage of determining intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*).

To explain: "Therefore, it is established that the validity of the means of knowledge, characterized by correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*), is ascertained from its own means of knowledge itself, without depending on the cognition of excellences (*guṇa*)."
And likewise: "It is known from its own cause alone," and similarly:
"The suchness of an object is a cognition that does not depend on a cognition of corroboration by qualities, because it is cognized even in the absence of those [qualities]," and so forth.
“Nor is the reason unestablished;
for instance, the ‘correspondence with reality’ of the cognition of silver consists in its having silver as its object,
and that is apprehended by the very cognition grasping the silver, provided there is no sublation,” and so forth.

Therefore, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of cognitions produced by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is known from their own cause as consisting precisely in the determination of an object as it actually exists; it does not depend upon a cognition of excellence (*guṇa*) or a corroborative cognition (*saṃvādajñāna*).
Thus, the validity of the means of knowledge consists precisely in their nature as the determination of an object as it actually exists.
The arguments appearing as those [of the opponent] are stated by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*);
even in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is precisely the demonstration of discrimination (*viveka*).
And if experience alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [then...]
That is neither logical nor useful;
nor do they treat every experience as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since this is not observed in cases such as the illusion of a yellow conch-shell.
Nor can all memory be considered invalid, for that would exclude those memories rooted in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, Varadaviṣṇumiśra’s statement that "valid cognition is that which has the capacity to grasp what has not been previously grasped" must also be understood as being made from the perspective of following the views of others.

As for what was stated in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*: "The intellect that pervades objects perceived through other means of valid cognition is itself a valid means of knowledge, provided it does not first contradict its own object."
Thus, this statement of restatement (*anuvādavākya*) is intended to exclude its own validity as a means of knowledge by virtue of being directed toward another purpose;

otherwise, in the case of a lapse of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*), where that specific aspect has been lost, since the apprehension of its own object cannot be established by prioritizing a prior experience, how could there be non-validity based on its being a memory? (Nyāyapariśuddhi, Śabdakhaṇḍa, p.
50). As for what was stated in the Bhāṣya during the refutation of perception that grasps only pure existence (*sanmātragrāhipratyakṣa*): "In the case of a horse..."

And [if one were to argue] that "in the case of the elephant and the two cognitions, because they have the same object, the subsequent [cognition] would be a grasping of what has already been grasped and would lack any distinction [from the first],

and thus it would not differ from memory"— [we reply that] in that context, the invalidity of memory was not indicated, since its distinction [from perception] is established by way of another criterion as well.
And because the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) arises in relation to that;

furthermore, as for the other commentary: "For this is the restriction of the nature of perception born of the sense faculties, namely, that it is the apprehender of an object existing at its own same time."
"But [this does not apply] to all cognitions and means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
because in cases such as memory, inference, scripture, and the yogic perception of practitioners, one observes the apprehension of even objects existing at a different time.
Regarding this, it is appropriate to provide a differentiated example by following the opponent's own intention in order to demonstrate an undesirable consequence for them.

Furthermore, as for what was stated in the *Śāstrayoni* section: “Even though that [knowledge] arising at the culmination of the intensification of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) possesses a vivid manifestation, it lacks validity because it is merely a memory of a previously experienced object;
how, then, can it be perception?”—this too does not represent the actual final position (*siddhānta*).
Nor has its correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*) been rejected therein;
other cases should be understood in the same way.

Even the Vaiśeṣikas, who maintain that memory is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), include it within the category of *vidyā* (correct knowledge) precisely because of its correspondence with reality.
For this very reason, even those who are partial adherents of that [system] have accepted its authority.

Thus ends the first section of the chapter on Smṛti in the Nyāyapariśuddhi, among the works of the venerable Vedāntācārya Śrī Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians, who is independent in all philosophical systems.
